column2: Act Seven
The Little Brother

They raced onward, with no destination in mind, simply following their whims, like a wandering swordsman and swordswoman who had gone crazy and smashed up somebody’s establishment, then decided to roam the world while everyone behind them shouted for their heads. As long as they ran fast enough, they could get away—if they were riding Jueying.
He wanted to capture this moment, to preserve their flight.
Only much later did he learn that Jueying was merely a legend. The Bugatti Veyron was the fastest production sports car in the world, but it could not outrun time, or a fate already sealed.
Number 13 crept, bent at the waist, along a pitch-black passage, holding his lit phone high and using the screen to light his way.
The vast network of passages resembled a maze. The only sound inside was the hum of extractor fans, repeating at a steady frequency.
Number 13 was beginning to regret taking this job.

He prided himself on being good at his trade. He had taken jobs exploring ancient tombs in deserts and shipwrecks in icy seas; every one of those places had been spookier than this college. His luck today had been pretty good, too. He had overcome every obstacle, and lucky coincidences kept coming his way. Lady Luck ought to be on his side. Yet for some reason, ever since entering this passage, he had felt something strange: an indefinable danger seemed to lie just ahead. A thought kept sounding in his mind: Don’t go any farther. Don’t go any farther.
He remembered the look the ghostly girl, transparent as crystal, had given him at the very last moment.
As though she were seeing a dead man off.
“Riiiiiiiiing…”
The phone rang in that dark, sealed space, vibrating too, and nearly frightened his heart to a stop. What cell provider had a signal that could reach dozens of meters underground?
There was no caller ID. The screen was a solid pale blue.
The phone wasn’t receiving a call!
Number 13 took several deep breaths, pressed Answer, and said nothing.

“This is a recording, not a phone call. Everything is proceeding according to our plan. Of course, if you have unfortunately died already, please turn off your phone. The following information will be of no use to you.” The flat voice coming from the phone belonged to the woman who gave him his instructions.
“How am I supposed to turn it off if I’m dead?” Number 13 muttered.
“That was a joke. I hope you understand that I’m trying to help you relax.” The woman continued, but her chilly tone made him want to flip a table.
“Please consult the map and enter the number corresponding to your current location, followed by the pound key,” she said.
“Come on, are you AT&T customer service?” Number 13 scratched his head.

A complete map of Cassell College appeared on the screen, like a magnificent spiderweb. Unlike the map Number 13 had found in the library, this was an underground cross section. It showed that the college’s subterranean buildings consisted of three major sections. Countless lines between them were passages linking the three; even the ventilation ducts were individually labeled, like innumerable threads spun by three enormous spiders. In one corner was the name of this level: “The Three Goddesses.”
“The three goddesses of fate?” Number 13 thought.

He had read Norse mythology. There were three such sisters among the Norse deities: Urd spun the thread of life, Verdandi drew it out, and Skuld cut it. This was the fate of all things in the world, and it could not be changed.
These passages were the threads on the map. Walking alone along a thread of fate felt at least a little inauspicious.

He found his position. He was traveling along a narrow, unbranching corridor labeled “13.” A mischievous thought occurred to him: he could enter another number and hear what instructions he got. Then again, if this important recorded guide only worked once, he would die a very ugly death.
He obediently pressed “13#.”
“Congratulations. You have reached the designated position as planned. The veil of the Three Goddesses will now be lifted.”

A thin, bright white line swept down the screen. Some passages were filtered out by the scan and turned gray, while others remained brilliant white. Every building’s name changed as well. The three principal complexes really were named after the three goddesses of fate. Number 13 suddenly noticed a pattern: every white passage began in the area marked “Urd,” passed through “Verdandi,” and finally led to “Skuld.” And from Skuld, who governed the future… there was no way out.
The map was steeped in fatalism. Life flowed in only one direction, from the past to the future, and from the future… there was no way out.
Did the designer of this college simply not believe in a future?
Number 13 felt a chill.
“Wait. Am I heading toward… the future?”
He realized something. His current position, “13,” lay precisely on a thread leading from Verdandi to Skuld: a thread already drawn out and measured, waiting for Skuld to cut it.
“The road to Skuld also leads to the ultimate secret. Your fee for this assignment has been increased to five million US dollars.”

Number 13’s spirits soared. Five million dollars was a truly enormous sum, five times the original fee! Once this job was done, he could retire. He wasn’t in this line of work to punish evil or uncover the mysteries of the universe. His reason was one simple word: money. He was a self-reliant sort, with no other particular talents and no tolerance for a life on welfare.
“Is the relative humidity close to one hundred percent? If yes, press ‘1#.’ If no, press ‘2#.’”
A fine layer of droplets covered the grip of his sawed-off shotgun. The cotton socks inside his boots were damp, and mist clouded his phone’s screen. The air here really was supersaturated.
Number 13 pressed “1#.”
“Is there an extremely strong residual magnetic field? If yes, press ‘1#.’ If no, press ‘2#.’”

Number 13 thought for a moment and pulled up his sleeve. His mechanical watch had stopped at 21:30, the time he entered the passage. There was undoubtedly an extremely powerful magnetic field here. But he had only ever heard that magnetized watches kept bad time, never that they stopped completely—unless the field was so strong that the gears and balance wheel were stuck fast together and could no longer come apart.
Number 13 pressed “1#.”
“Does the air smell of rusting metal? If yes, press ‘1#.’ If no, press ‘2#.’”
A pungent smell of rust filled the air. Number 13 pressed “1#.”

“Based on these results, you are now extremely close to the target,” the woman said. “Continue forward. Locate, observe, and record the target. Remember, you must see the target yourself. You must look directly at it with your naked eyes! You do not need to remove it. Your report alone is worth five million dollars. When you see the target, you will receive your final instructions.”

Number 13’s delight reached its peak. He didn’t even have to take the target out; observation, notes, and a report alone were worth five million. What a job! The shadow over his heart vanished in an instant.
“Good luck, Number 13,” the woman said softly.

The recording ended. Number 13 put the phone in his trouser pocket and trudged on. The farther he went, the damper the air grew. Water condensed on the ceiling and fell in sharp little splats. The water underfoot gradually rose above the soles of his boots. He was no longer an elegant bat, merely a water rat in a sewer.
“Good luck, Number 13.” He suddenly remembered the woman’s last words.
Strange. That last sentence had actually been addressed to him alone. He had thought the recorded guide was intended for everyone on the team.
Valhalla.
Team B had complete control of the area. Its members were the backbone of the Student Council, and most had attended the ball at Amber Hall.

There had been no time to change out of their little black evening dresses or white gauzy court gowns. The girls pinned up their hair, tied up their hems, and carried Uzis with thirty-round magazines of nine-millimeter ammunition. Loaded spare magazines hung over their right shoulders, and pistols were strapped tightly to their thighs beneath their skirts. Astonishingly, they still wore rhinestone-studded high heels.
“The splendor of Gothic beauties!” A Student Council officer gazed through a patterned window, her long white dress swaying in the wind.

Eight students who had excelled in Battlefield Survival II held the front entrance, eight the rear, and four each of the side entrances. Two stood beneath each patterned floor-to-ceiling window. Six more waited in the second-floor passage, equipped with light and heavy weapons, ready to reinforce any position at a moment’s notice.
Inside the hall, Caesar Gattuso, president of the Cassell College Student Council, sat quietly with his eyes closed, resting.

Valhalla was an ancient Byzantine-style building in the center of Odin Square. Its exterior was faced with granite streaked in dark red. Rumor said the stone came from India, where a dragon-slaying war had once spilled the blood of humans and dragons alike. The blood had seeped into the local granite beds. Hundreds of years later, quarrymen discovered the stone’s unusual color, with crimson filling its grain. A complete image of the World Tree was carved across the outer walls. A rooster stood at its summit; at its roots lay imprisoned the ancestor of all dragons, the black dragon Nidhogg.

It was something like a sanctuary at Cassell College, used for the conferral of degrees. Normally it opened only once a year. Students entered in academic robes modeled on Prussian court dress and sat in rows of oak pews, waiting for the principal to call their names. Then, amid everyone’s applause, they went up to receive their degrees. Portraits of heroes who had rendered great service to humanity in the dragon-slaying wars lined the walls on either side.
Caesar sat in the front row, wearing an exquisite white suit, his head tilted back toward the statue beneath the circular dome.
It was Odin: armored from head to foot, mounted on an eight-legged warhorse, spear in hand.
His hunting knife, Dictator, lay quietly across his knees. A pair of fully loaded Desert Eagles rested on the seat beside him.
His eyes were closed. He chewed a strip of beef jerky, a faint smile at the corners of his mouth.

Every sound in Valhalla and within several hundred meters of it echoed in his mind: mosquitoes rubbing their wings in the air, tiny insects wriggling through the soil, and the forty-six differently paced heartbeats of the forty-six people under his command. Suddenly there were fifty-eight. An instant earlier, twelve unfamiliar heartbeats had entered Caesar’s domain.
Yanling: Kamaitachi.
Caesar opened his eyes, took out his phone, and dialed.
“Chu Zihang, what are you doing right now?” he asked.
“I don’t know. There’s nothing to do. Just waiting, I suppose.” Chu Zihang’s voice came from the other end.
“My guests are here. How about yours?”
“What’s coming will come.”
“Who’s going to finish the fight first? What should we bet this time?”
“You lost your sports car on Freedom Day. I lost my sword. Neither of us has handed over the stakes to the winner, Lu Mingfei. Why bother making another bet?”
“Fair point.” Caesar thought of the Bugatti Veyron parked in his garage. As far as he knew, the car was still sitting obediently there.

He felt a little downhearted. It wasn’t that he begrudged the car; he simply felt too awkward to drive it up to Lu Mingfei and hand it over. His original plan had been that, if Lu Mingfei obediently came onstage and stood beside him, he would casually pull the key from his pocket, slap it into Lu Mingfei’s palm, and say, “This toy should have been yours all along.” Even imagining that moment made Caesar a little nervous. What if Lu Mingfei refused?
Chu Zihang hung up.
Caesar lowered his head again, closed his eyes, and rested his forehead in his hands.
The chapel.
This was Team C’s area. Team C was much smaller than Team B, but more elite: all twenty members belonged to the Lionheart Society.

The Lionheart Society’s elite were the college’s veteran fighting force. The moment they received their diplomas, the doors of the Executive Department would open to them. These elites did not hold fixed positions; they stayed constantly on the move. Anyone trying to enter the building would discover that a different squad blocked each entrance at every moment. The coordination between squads had been rehearsed countless times and was seamless.
Behind a carved screen stood the confessional of the Cassell College chapel. Chu Zihang had remained inside it the whole time.

A black-clad figure leaped down from the second floor. Susie, serving as a sniper, approached the confessional. She was twenty-one, a third-year, A-rank, specializing in Dragon Genetics. She was an important member and vice president of the Lionheart Society, as well as Nono’s roommate, which made her quite well known. Whenever people compared Chu Zihang and Caesar, they invariably compared Nono and Susie as well. The two girls maintained peace in everyday life and absolute opposition in their loyalties to their respective groups.
“Everything okay?” Susie knocked on the confessional door.
“Fine. Things are about to start on Caesar’s side. It shouldn’t be long here, either,” Chu Zihang said from inside.
“Your health…”
“Perfect. Nothing wrong at all,” Chu Zihang interrupted.
“Team C, acknowledge and withdraw from the chapel area. Team C, acknowledge and withdraw from the chapel area.” Professor von Schneider’s voice sounded over Team C’s shared channel.
“Yes, sir!” everyone answered together.

Obedience had become second nature to them. The Lionheart Society had closer ties to the Executive Department than the Student Council did. Its members could practically be called the department’s reserve force.
“Zihang! We’re withdrawing.” Susie knocked on the confessional door again.

The order puzzled her. The chapel was the main junction leading to the Three Goddesses level and the clock tower where the Night Watcher lived. They should have been concentrating their defenses here.
“No. That doesn’t include me,” Chu Zihang said quietly.
“Doesn’t include you?” Susie froze. “The order went out to everyone over the shared channel.”
“Team C, acknowledge and withdraw from the chapel area immediately. This excludes Chu Zihang.” Professor von Schneider’s voice sounded again. Chu Zihang seemed to have expected this order all along.
“That order is only for people who don’t need to take part in the fight in the chapel,” Chu Zihang said. “Susie, withdraw.”
He reached out from behind the curtain and firmly clasped Susie’s wrist. His hand was pale, slender, warm, and strong.
“Don’t worry. Unless something unexpected happens, we can have a late-night snack together in two hours,” he said.
“Is that a promise?” Susie laid her hand over his.
“Yes.”
Professor von Schneider watched the dots representing Team C withdraw from the chapel on the large screen and let out a heavy sigh.
“You’re leaving Chu Zihang there alone?” Professor Guderian was shocked by the order. “That’s too much responsibility for a second-year student!”
“Who is Chu Zihang’s adviser?” Schneider asked.
“You.”

“Correct. I am Chu Zihang’s adviser.” Schneider nodded. “So I know what my student is capable of. Edict has been lifted. The students’ Yanling have been unsealed. They are wild horses on the grasslands now, with limitless possibilities.”
“Chu Zihang’s Yanling… what is it?” Guderian had realized something.
Schneider hesitated for an instant. His voice turned brutally cold. “Only a student’s adviser and the principal are authorized to consult that student’s Yanling file. You have no right to ask!”

“Chu Zihang’s Yanling… is very dangerous?” Manstein stood behind Schneider and put a hand on his shoulder, his gaze stern. “You ordered the rest of Team C out because you don’t want anyone to know his Yanling. They’re all members of the Lionheart Society; they wouldn’t reveal a secret lightly. Yet you still don’t want them to know… because it’s dangerous. Isn’t that right?”
“I repeat: you have no right to inquire!” Schneider’s face was expressionless.

“You never reported this to the Disciplinary Committee! Don’t talk nonsense. Ordinary professors have no right to inspect Yanling files, but I can request special access in the committee’s name! Have you forgotten the school regulations? Damn it!” Manstein raised his voice. “Schneider! You head the Executive Department. You should understand what our students are! They carry both human and dragon blood. When they issue commands within their domains, they change the laws of nature. Case after case has proved how dangerous these powers are. Do you remember the real reason that student we said ‘shot himself’ died?”
“I reported this to the principal. He tacitly allowed me to keep it confidential,” Schneider said quietly. “Manstein, do me a favor and forget this. Chu Zihang’s Yanling is still under my control.”

“Damn it! Whether you can control it isn’t the issue! School regulations require every dangerous Yanling ability to be formally registered. Simply telling the principal isn’t enough. He has no authority to give you tacit permission, either! If I keep quiet about this and the board finds out, all four of us—you, me, the principal, and Guderian—will have broken the rules!” Manstein was furious. “You can control it now, but how can you guarantee it won’t go out of control in the future? How can we have no contingency plan?”
Schneider was silent for a long time. He drew a deep breath. “Chu Zihang… is a good student.”
“That has nothing to do with whether he’s a good student!”
“Once his Yanling is judged to pose a risk, he’ll be isolated from all the other students. Correct?” Schneider looked into Manstein’s eyes.
“Yes.”

“I believe Chu Zihang is a good student, working hard to adjust to his ability and become one of us. We have all experienced the loneliness of blood sorrow. He came to Cassell College to overcome that loneliness. I can think of no reason not to help him,” Schneider said quietly. “I was once isolated because my Yanling was dangerous. I know that pain. You both know it too, from the children’s psychiatric hospital. Don’t you?”
The room fell silent. Manstein and Guderian looked at each other. Neither spoke.

“Chu Zihang is a good student, just as Lu Mingfei is a good student. And I have never heard a thing about descendants of the White King.” Schneider stared at them both, a cold light in his iron-gray eyes.
“Wh-what descendants of the White King?” Guderian’s tongue seemed to tie itself in knots.

There had always been a shadow over his heart. He had never seen Lu Mingfei’s answers on the 3E exam. After grading them, Norma had reported the results directly to the principal, who had personally announced that Lu Mingfei had passed. That amounted to an endorsement of his bloodline. But it could not explain why Lu Mingfei had failed to react to Yanling: Emperor. He had resonated with all sorts of high-level Yanling during the exam, yet remained unmoved by Emperor, the symbol of the Black King’s bloodline.
He did not submit to Emperor.
Of all the dragons recorded in history, only the White King’s descendants did not submit to Emperor.

But Guderian had said nothing, and Manstein had never brought it up again. No one at Cassell College had studied Dragon Genealogy more deeply than those two. If they “just happened” to overlook the same detail, no one else should have noticed it. Schneider should not have noticed it, either. That night, he had seemed to believe Manstein’s explanation. Given his temperament, he would certainly have raised any suspicions instead of hiding them. Gradually, Guderian had relaxed.

“Manstein, you aren’t very good at lying. Your excuse was excellent, but your wandering eyes gave you away. Guderian scratches his head when he lies. You look down and to the right. You really are graduates of the same psychiatric hospital; even your bad habits are alike. To borrow a Chinese saying, when you mock him, you’re a man who fled fifty paces laughing at a man who fled a hundred!” Schneider looked into Manstein’s eyes. “As soon as you left the library, I went back, pulled up the archive room’s surveillance footage, watched your entire argument from beginning to end, and destroyed the recording.”

Manstein quietly sat down at the table and turned toward his old friend Guderian. “Even the head of the Disciplinary Committee wouldn’t be forgiven by the board for breaking the rules like this, would he?”
“I can forgive it,” Schneider said softly. “The three of us can have an understanding.”
“You mean…?” Guderian’s eyes lit up.

“Your good student Lu Mingfei and my good student Chu Zihang are both fine, hardworking, perfectly normal young men. They deserve the most complete education this campus can provide, instead of being isolated as freaks. They will become heroes of Cassell College, and of humanity itself.” Schneider spoke very slowly. “Isn’t that right?”
Guderian and Manstein stared at one another, unable to react for a moment.
“Exactly right! No question about it!” Guderian suddenly understood. He stood up and spoke loudly.
“Excellent. That makes us both outstanding advisers.” A rare smile appeared on Schneider’s scarred face. “And the chair of the Disciplinary Committee agrees with us, I trust?”

“Hey! What does either of you being an outstanding adviser have to do with me? Lu Mingfei is Guderian’s student, and Chu Zihang is yours. This never had anything to do with me in the first place, did it?” Manstein protested. “Yet somehow I’ve been dragged in and have to help you lie? I’m getting the short end of the stick here, aren’t I?”

“Not really. You have a new student. As far as I know, her Yanling file is rather unusual, too. It’s just that the principal has kept it under wraps, so it has never been studied in depth.” Schneider patted Manstein on the shoulder.

“Who? What new student?” Manstein was stunned. He was one of the few professors without students under his supervision and only taught classes. Serving concurrently as head of the Disciplinary Committee already kept him extremely busy.
“Chen Motong.” Schneider pronounced the name slowly. “Her previous adviser, Mans, designated you to succeed him. Would you like to know what’s in her Yanling file?”
“Mans… why did he choose me?” Manstein was dumbfounded.

“Two reasons. First, she does campus work with Guderian, and you’re Guderian’s friend, so you’re bound to look after her. Second, one of your committee’s responsibilities is to monitor Yanling, and you have privileged access to the files. If you become her adviser… Well, although you’re both greedy and sharp-tongued, you have remarkably little backbone…”
“Greedy, sharp-tongued, spineless… what exactly are you trying to say?” Manstein sounded helpless.

“You protect the people close to you. It’s a habit of yours. According to her file, Chen Motong… has no Yanling!” Schneider said slowly. “An A-rank student, yet Mans claimed she had no Yanling. Even F-rank Fingel has one. And Mans blocked any investigation into her. There’s only one explanation, isn’t there? Her Yanling is special—so special he couldn’t put it in the file. Mans was very fond of that student. You both know that.”
“Damn it… I’m already busy enough. Why hand her to me? And why should I protect her? I could simply write an honest report and submit it to the principal,” Manstein said.
Schneider drew a deep breath and said softly, “You won’t mistreat Chen Motong. Think of it as fulfilling… her mother’s request to you.”
Manstein was silent for a long time. He said nothing.
“You don’t have a Yanling?” Lu Mingfei was curious.

He and Nono were on their way back to the college. Nono was driving, and a woman on the car stereo was merrily singing, “Fight, fight, fight the landlord.” Nono’s MP3 player held all sorts of strange songs: rap, mysterious Nordic themes, hymns, and this ubiquitous “Fight, fight, fight the landlord.” After the fireworks, they were both giddy with happiness.

Nono said she collected music like a scavenger walking down the street with a basket on her back. Whenever she saw something good, she tossed it into the basket, never sorting or organizing anything. When she had time, she turned the basket upside down, dumped all her finds on the ground, and rummaged through this and that with no system whatsoever. Lu Mingfei admired her approach. He, too, had once longed for the utterly carefree life of a scavenger.
“I really don’t, although a lot of people don’t believe me.” Nono shrugged. “I resonate with Draconic, but I can’t control a Yanling. It gave Professor Mans headaches, too.”
“How many kinds of Yanling are there?” Slouched in the passenger seat, Lu Mingfei watched the wind whip Nono’s long hair into a dark red flame.

“One hundred eighteen have been recorded so far. Together they form something like the periodic table. The higher a Yanling’s sequence number, the less stable and more dangerous it is, and the worse the backlash on the person using it,” Nono said. “They’ll teach you all that in Introduction to Yanling next semester.”
“So what’s the most awesome one?”

“I don’t know. All Yanling above number eighty-eight are unstable. Eighty-nine through one hundred are classified as ‘dangerous,’ one hundred one through one hundred twelve as ‘high-risk,’ and everything from one hundred thirteen onward as ‘top secret.’”
“Top secret?”

“It means that even if those Yanling have been observed, their information isn’t made public. Their danger can’t be calculated. The most dangerous one I know of is number one hundred twelve, Rhine. Someone used it in Tunguska in the nineteenth century. A squad of dragon slayers went into Tunguska, and not one came out alive. A shock wave resembling a nuclear explosion was observed there. Hundreds of qing of forest—thousands of acres—were flattened, and the light could be seen as far away as the Rhine. That’s why it’s called Rhine. The Research Department believes Rhine is a Yanling with an enormous energy demand. It lasted only 0.003 seconds before its user was utterly drained.”
“The… the Tunguska explosion?”
“Yep. At Cassell College, that incident is called the Rhine Conflagration.”
“A power that badass only ranks one hundred twelve?” Lu Mingfei was dumbfounded. “Then what’s number one hundred eighteen? It’s got to be a twenty-times Kaio-ken!”
“No way. It’s definitely a Super Saiyan transformation!” Nono shook her head, joining him in talking nonsense.

“Do you have a Yanling like the Kamehameha?” Lu Mingfei struck a pose. “Watch, watch, like this. One person drives, the other sits in the passenger seat firing Kamehamehas. Wouldn’t that make it a tank? Boom!” He thrust both hands forward.
Imagining the scene he described, Nono burst out laughing, and the steering wheel wobbled.
“Careful, careful! Don’t let happiness turn into traaaaagedy!” Lu Mingfei shouted.

For a while, neither spoke. The headlights lit the dark mountain road, and the cries of wild owls swept overhead. They rode in a sports car, the boy in a rented suit and the girl in a purple skirt suit. The wind rushed straight at them, lifting their hair—his tousled, hers streaming. Up on the mountainside, people were fighting and killing, while their car played the cheerful “Fight, fight, fight the landlord.”
“Big sis, can your phone take pictures?” Lu Mingfei suddenly asked.
Nono tossed him her iPhone. “No snooping through my texts.”
“Come on, let’s take a picture together.” He waved the phone.
“Hey, don’t mess around! We’re doing sixty kilometers an hour on a mountain road. How are we supposed to pose for a picture?”
“You don’t have to move. I can just turn sideways.” Lu Mingfei turned and, without consulting her, leaned halfway against Nono, stretching one arm far out to take a selfie.

He wondered how many moments like this he would have in his lifetime. The speeding car left everything else in the world behind. Against the backdrop of other people’s battles, a boy and a girl raced like lightning, laughing and talking loudly, as if they were fleeing—or eloping.

He had heard that Cao Cao owned a magnificent horse called Jueying, so fast that even its shadow could not catch it. Lu Mingfei imagined the horse with a coat of pure gold, running forever in sunlight, the border between light and darkness always behind it. Whenever the darkness was about to catch up, it would break into a wild gallop again. But when he played Dynasty Warriors, he discovered that they had actually made the horse black.

They raced onward, with no destination in mind, simply following their whims, like a wandering swordsman and swordswoman who had gone crazy and smashed up somebody’s establishment, then decided to roam the world while everyone behind them shouted for their heads. As long as they ran fast enough, they could get away—if they were riding Jueying.
He wanted to capture this moment, to preserve their flight.
Only much later did he learn that Jueying was merely a legend. The Bugatti Veyron was the fastest production sports car in the world, but it could not outrun time, or a fate already sealed.
Just as he pressed the shutter, Nono took one hand off the wheel and pinched his nose hard, turning her head in a flash to stick out her tongue and make a face.
Click. Lu Mingfei’s startled, wide-eyed face was frozen in a tiny speck of flash memory, Nono’s arm crossing his neck and gripping it tight.

Number 13 was still slogging along. He had better get ready to swim. The passage began to slope downward, and droplets rattled down from the ceiling until he might as well have been walking through a downpour. The water was knee-deep, and every step took effort. A red light blinked ahead. He guessed he was nearing the end.

The floor vanished beneath him. With nothing to stand on, he floated free in the water. It was icy and salty, like seawater, though at least it was clean and clear. Number 13 took a deep breath and dived. He regretted it immediately. His shotgun ammunition would certainly be useless once soaked. Worse still, there was the phone.

He hurried to the surface, shook the water off the phone, and jabbed at the power button. But the water had evidently soaked through the battery. No matter how hard he pressed, it showed no sign of life. His employer had mailed it directly to him before the mission. It was an ordinary, inexpensive model, but he still hadn’t received the final instruction. From here on, he was on his own.
All he had to do was find the target and write a report anyway! And Number 13 was pretty good at reports. He honed his prose by writing battle reports on real-time strategy gaming sites.
He threw the phone into the water, dived again, and swam slowly toward the blinking red light.
The phone sank gently and lodged in a crack.

Number 13 finally reached the red light. It stood beside an antiquated sluice gate at the end of the passage. The gate was brass and badly corroded. Stamped in German along an edge were the date and the name of the factory that had cast it. The year was 1912, nearly a century earlier. Back then, Germany’s casting technology had been the most advanced in the world. Shipping this thing across the ocean to America must have cost a fortune.
1912. A long, long time ago.
Number 13 gripped the gate handle, wondering what he would see when he opened it. That hateful feeling returned, as though opening this gate would cause something terrible to happen.
That feeling when everything is perfectly normal, yet you desperately want to abandon five million dollars, turn around, and flee the way you came.
“Brother.”

Goose bumps sprang up all over his body, and he whipped around. No one was behind him, only the sound of rippling water. Was he hearing things? He had no little brother. He was an orphan, alone through and through.
He leaned against the gate and accidentally pressed the handle down.
“Ah!” he screamed.

The gate burst open. In an instant he lost his balance and fell with tens, hundreds of tons of salt water, like someone shooting over Niagara Falls in a tiny kayak. Number 13 squeezed his eyes shut until a splash engulfed him in bubbles. He had landed in water.

He slowly opened his eyes and looked around. He was submerged in pale blue water, contained by towering glass walls. Ice-blue lamps were embedded in the glass, their light refracting and shifting through this world of water and glass. It looked rather familiar.
“An… aquarium?” He realized he had fallen into an aquarium tank.

He had once visited an aquarium in Brooklyn with a cheerleader from his high school class who liked marine life, to look at sea turtles. But afterward the cheerleader had refused to date him again, so he had stopped going to aquariums. Now he was seeing one from a sea turtle’s perspective. It felt quite different from looking in through the glass.
“A tank this big—is it for sea turtles? Or…” Number 13 suddenly shuddered. He realized the tank was much too big.
“Sharks?” That completed his sentence.

He turned slowly. Behind him, a pair of eyes the size of Ping-Pong balls was watching him curiously. A genuine great white shark. Perhaps to prove it was a young shark with a perfectly functional set of jaws, the great white slowly opened its mouth, displaying a thicket of teeth.
“Come on… if you’ve got the guts!” Number 13 said shakily.

The shark did not attack. Moving its fins and tail gently, it retreated in silence. The distance between them slowly increased, like a wolf making a calculated withdrawal in the face of a wild boar. At about ten meters, the great white abruptly turned, dived at high speed, and shot into a hole in an artificial reef. A moment later, a red cloud of blood rose from the hole, followed by a large dead fish tossed outside. The shark had killed the fish and taken its cave, apparently seeking shelter.
“Told you you didn’t have the guts!” Number 13 panted.

This was an ability he had been born with, and the reason the beautiful cheerleader had rejected him. No animal dared approach him, from rabbits to sea turtles. As a child, he had stood beside a rabbit cage with a carrot for hours, but the rabbit only huddled in a corner, panting nonstop.
“Am I just someone nobody likes?” Number 13 had always felt terribly inferior as a child.
This time, though, he was deeply grateful for that trait.
He swam hard toward the glass wall. His grappling gun proved its worth again, and he climbed the rope and scrambled over.
“Cassell College. Aquatic Habitat Seven. Principal resident species: Pliosauroidea,” he read from the sign on the glass.

Number 13 had no idea what the Greek-derived word “Pliosauroidea” meant, so he simply assumed it was the biological classification for great white sharks. Thus he also confused predator and prey in the enormous seawater tank. He had never seen the tank’s true master.
He threaded his way cautiously through the passages between the glass walls. After who knew how long, he finally saw a sign at the end of the underwater tunnel:
“Ice Cellar”!
The captain stood silently beside a patterned window in Valhalla.

Not far from him, two second-years holding Uzis stared outside with hawklike eyes, ready to meet an attack at any moment, yet they showed no reaction to the twelve people clustered beside them. Even if they concentrated, they would only have seen a faint, swirling, ink-dark current in the air, like a ghost.
The other eleven pressed tightly against their captain, practically wishing they could glue themselves to him. Packed together like this, they had shuffled into Valhalla in tiny steps.

It was an extremely uncomfortable way to walk, but they had no better option. The domain of Yanling: Dark Illumination was a circle only two meters in radius around its user. They huddled like a flower, with their captain at its center.
The captain looked at two photographs hanging side by side on the wall.
“Ye Sheng. Assistant Agent, Executive Department, Cassell College. March 1985–October 2009.”
“Aki Sakatoku. Assistant Agent, Executive Department, Cassell College. December 1986–October 2009.”

The boy and girl in the photographs were both Asian. The boy had a sunny face, his downturned mouth bearing a hint of a mischievous grin. The girl had gentle features and warm eyes, with soft bangs covering her forehead: the very image of the girl next door. Both photographs had been cropped and enlarged from the same large picture, something like a graduation group photo. They wore identical academic gowns against the same amber sunlight. In the distance behind them stood this ancient, mysterious Valhalla.
The other eleven did not understand why the captain had stopped to examine photographs of dragon-slaying heroes. But they could only wait. They all knew his temper.
The captain sighed soundlessly and moved up the central aisle toward the statue of Odin. An extremely faint black haze flowed along the aisle.

Everyone in Team B was looking outside except the boy resting with his eyes closed on an oak pew. He wore a white suit and had hair as brilliant as gold. One hand rested on a black hunting knife. Two enormous silver Desert Eagles lay beside him. They were custom pistols, with grips of carved ebony inlaid with ivory and a solid silver family crest in the center.
That blond hair was truly dazzling. Approaching him from behind, the captain had a strong urge to smack his head and feel whether it was a wig.
He suppressed the thought and passed in silence. The boy’s head was bowed, a faint smile at his lips. He seemed to have noticed nothing.

It was a raid without the slightest challenge. Success that came too easily was always a little dull. The captain and his companions stood in the center of Valhalla, the pride of Cassell College, before the black velvet curtain beneath Odin’s statue, while the enemy was dozing. He felt an urge to teach the youngsters the meaning of professionalism.
Caesar opened his eyes, raised his head, and smiled at the statue of Odin.
When this boy who looked like a Greek statue smiled, there was something between elegance and cruelty about him. The leader started.

Caesar was looking straight at them, but the countless trials of Yanling: Dark Illumination gave the captain ample confidence. Against a black background, human vision could never detect the faint dark currents left by Dark Illumination.
“When our class receives its degrees, will I be the first to walk up to the podium?” Caesar said casually.
The captain had no idea whom he was asking. Perhaps the statue of Odin behind him.

Had they been detected? Given his temperament, he hardly minded a fight, but whether they had actually been discovered, and whether he should end his Yanling and leap out to fight, was another matter. If Caesar was only talking to himself on a whim, jumping out would look stupid. He hesitated.
Music suddenly pierced the silence.

A grand melody echoed through Valhalla, not loud, but loud enough for everyone to hear. They all turned in surprise toward Odin’s statue, unable to locate the source. The lilting tune sounded like something the campus broadcasting system would play at afternoon tea.
“‘Ashitaka Sekki,’ from the score to Hayao Miyazaki’s Princess Mononoke. I’m rather fond of it myself,” Caesar said mildly.
The music beneath the black curtain stopped, replaced by an irritated girl’s voice. “Hey! Who is this? Calling me now—are you trying to get yourself killed?”
Yanling: Dark Illumination, deactivated.

Twelve people appeared at once. They wore unmarked black combat uniforms, carried compact submachine guns, and had two-foot close-combat blades at their waists. Hoods and masks covered everything but their hawklike eyes.

Team B immediately recognized the campus intruders, clearly the elite of the elite. They should have opened fire at once, but froze. The enemy was in a bizarre formation: eleven men crowded around the sole woman, crouching and linking arms, as though performing some African tribal courtship dance.
“Get lost! Why are you still sticking so close?” The captain, the team’s only woman, planted a hand on a companion’s head and shoved him away.

The eleven scattered and instantly assumed combat positions behind the surrounding pews and podium, raising their compact submachine guns. At the same time, Team B’s main forces poured in from the front and rear entrances, while black gun barrels appeared between the balusters on the top floor.
A net with no escape.

Both sides chambered rounds with a precision that sounded rehearsed. The slightest pull of a trigger would unleash a torrent of bullets. At the same moment, however, Caesar and the woman both raised their hands, halting any further action.
Caesar made a graceful gesture indicating that the captain could finish her call. Without so much as looking at him, she continued talking, running her hand through her long black ponytail.
“Green Forest? Do we know each other? Where did you get my number?” the captain demanded into her phone.
“Oh…” She seemed to remember something and glanced at Caesar. “Yes, I booked your services through Mint, but I did not request a follow-up call.”

“What? Nono?” She frowned. “No! Don’t you have a customer service representative with better hearing? Have you never had Asian customers before? Your spelling is simply… All right, all right, I’m in a very bad mood. Please stop wasting the time I have with my client… no, with my competitor. Tell your marketing department they need people who understand Chinese! Otherwise take ‘International’ out of your company name!”
She stabbed a button and ended the call. “I hate people who aren’t professional!” She shrugged at Caesar. “I can’t stand these so-called luxury concierge clubs. They actually gave out my number.”
“Mint? I’m a member, too.” Caesar took out his wallet and produced a black card bearing the word “Mint” in silver.

Mint was a famous luxury concierge club serving the very wealthiest clients. Paupers like Lu Mingfei had never even heard its name. It had branches in Cannes, Hong Kong, and Shanghai. Membership could fulfill any desire within human capability. For example, suppose you finished dinner in New York at six in the evening, belched contentedly, and suddenly decided to fly to Japan for that night’s performance at Tokyo’s Kabuki-za. In theory, no scheduled flight could get you there in time, and even the standing-room tickets were sold out. No problem. Call Mint. Then finish your coffee, step outside, and get into a car. A Concorde would be waiting at the airport.
That was Mint. Very much Caesar’s style, and very much the girl captain’s style, too.
The elites on both sides, weapons clenched in their hands, exchanged glances. At a moment like this, their commanders had actually begun discussing the service at some luxury club.

“I had no choice. It was a simple job, but the boss gave us too little time. It looked impossible without calling them.” The captain shrugged indifferently. “You don’t need to show me your card. And don’t expect to find me through the club.”
“I’m merely curious about our opponents. Are dragons a bunch of bad-tempered women who shop through Mint?” Caesar studied the leader’s face. “You look very familiar.”
“Aki Sakatoku’s older sister. Mai Sakatoku.” The captain glanced at the photograph on the wall. “You must have met my little sister.”

No one, even an enemy, could deny she was beautiful—one in ten thousand. In high heels, she might have stood taller than Caesar. Her close-fitting combat uniform distilled every curve of her body. Had she modeled for a drawing class, teacher and students alike would have needed plugs of tissue in both nostrils to work. Her long black hair was tied in a ponytail, baring a pale, slender nape like a girl practicing kendo. Her radiant face always seemed to say, “Ugh, why does everything have to be such a hassle?” The long outer corners of her lightly shaded eyes were like crimson blades.
Compared with Aki Sakatoku’s delicate loveliness, her older sister’s beauty was a stroke of intoxicating red beneath a painter’s brush.
“You aren’t twins, I take it?” Caesar assessed her for a moment.

“We are. Biologically speaking, just not identical. Otherwise she wouldn’t have been such an ugly duckling, always lacking confidence.” The captain spoke as though discussing something unrelated to herself, turning to look out the window.
She seemed a little unhappy now, making her beauty more real. That expression made the boys aiming guns at her feel a little embarrassed to shoot.
“You won’t even cover your face? You don’t mind openly announcing who you are? Apparently people really do regard Cassell College as somewhere they can drop by for a sightseeing tour,” Caesar said.
“I tried masks before, but they weren’t much use.” Mai gave her habitual shrug. “People remember my figure better than my face. I can hardly drape myself from head to toe in an Arab robe.”
Caesar nodded slightly. “True. Especially men. It would be difficult not to remember.”

For Mai, excessive physical perfection was her greatest flaw. Even if every girl present put on a white gauzy court gown and stood in a row, Mai’s commanding figure would instantly draw every man’s eyes.

“All right, what exactly are you getting at? Let’s fight.” Mai was losing patience. She curled her lip. “Don’t expect grief over losing my sister to give you an opening. Aki and I didn’t grow up together, so we didn’t have much of a sisterly bond. Besides, I’m completely different from an ugly duckling like her.”
“I can see that.” Caesar nodded. “How would you like to begin?”
Mai took out her phone and set it on the podium beside her. “How about a Western? When the music ends, we start.”
“‘Ashitaka Sekki’?” Caesar asked.
“Yes. ‘Ashitaka Sekki.’ You know it, and so do I. The instant it ends, we begin.” Mai pressed Play.

Caesar rose, unbuttoned his suit jacket, and picked up a Desert Eagle in each hand. Mai lifted her eyebrows. Suddenly she shone, dazzling as the cold gleam of a blade, so menacing that no one would dare approach. Behind each of them stood more than ten loaded guns aimed at the other side, with over a thousand rounds in their magazines.

The music began. It was like being deep in a forest ten thousand years old, with countless fireflies dancing while spirits sang an ancient lament. So much loneliness, so much sorrow, gathered into a grandeur like a mountain.

“This track is two minutes thirty-nine seconds long. Team C, your nearest backup, needs four minutes to get here. In the one minute twenty-one seconds after the music ends, which of us do you think will still be standing?” Mai looked into Caesar’s ice-blue eyes. The surging, blade-like aura around her was growing stronger.

“No one will reinforce this position unless I fall. Everyone will remain at their posts, guarding every entrance to the Three Goddesses level. We won’t fall for a diversion. According to the surveillance footage, there are thirteen of you, and I see only twelve here.”
“Very sharp, but not quite accurate. There are two more. Professor von Schneider certainly has every confidence you can handle things here.”
“Would you mind telling me where the other two are headed?”
“One went toward the chapel. The other seems to be getting lost.”

The music played on. Amid the mingled strings and winds, spirits sang with tears flying, and fireflies scattered in every direction. The voice of a bowed fiddle broke free of the surrounding sound. Helplessness rose like a mountain piled above the clouds; a lonely child carried a lamp that could not illuminate the way home.
The commanders continued their leisurely conversation, both seeming somewhat distracted by the music. A murderous tension began to spread between the two teams.
“Thank you.” Caesar smiled.

“There’s no harm in telling you. It’s already too late for you to do anything. The woman giving the orders may spend all her time munching chips and directing us remotely, looking like she takes nothing seriously, but deep down she’s a queen through and through. Her orders make no logical sense, and she demands one hundred percent obedience, but she has never made a mistake in planning. As for the girl going to find Chu Zihang, she’s an ice-cold, three-nothings girl. She always wears a cold expression and can never work with anyone, but as far as I know, she has never failed an assignment.” Mai shrugged. “By comparison, you should count yourself lucky. I’m the easiest person on this team to get along with.”
“What is your objective?”
“The skeletal remains of the Dragon King Norton.”
“Very candid. Anything else?”
“A new era.”
“A new era? Do you consider yourselves revolutionaries? You want a new era like… Japan after the Meiji Restoration?”
“Far newer than that,” Mai said softly. Suddenly a misty haze drifted through her beautiful eyes, and behind it lay a splendor that took the breath away.
“Seeing the longing for that era in a pair of beautiful eyes makes me look forward to it myself.” Caesar lowered his head.

He began counting silently. The music had passed its final climax. The last sustained note would last fifteen seconds, like a forest keeper silent for thousands of years, gazing down an endless road with deeply wrinkled eyes. He felt grateful that, besides his love of Puccini, he had also studied Japanese anime scores.
The music broke off as though severed by a blade!

Eleven guns fired as one. Each precisely delivered two three-round bursts, sixty-six bullets in all. The music had ended abruptly, without the expected fifteen-second sustained note. Mai Sakatoku’s version of “Ashitaka Sekki” ended in a soaring march.

Before any Team B student could pull a trigger, a bullet was already flying toward them. In the intruders’ hands, what should have been impossible for ordinary people became reality. A three-round burst was meant to form a small barrage in the air, the bullets closely spaced to tear a target apart, their trajectories forming a triangle. But in these intruders’ hands, the trajectories diverged completely. Each burst struck three targets instead of one!
One second of stunned hesitation, and the battle tilted decisively to one side.
Without a thought, Mai drew her Glock and aimed at the center of Caesar’s forehead. She only ever fired the one decisive shot, killing the enemy commander.
Blood-red spray blossomed in the air, like countless red flowers opening at the same instant. Team B’s students had been hit in vital spots, and had not yet had time to fall…
But where Mai’s muzzle pointed, Caesar had vanished.
Yanling: Kamaitachi. Twelve intruders, twelve heartbeats. Positions confirmed.

Caesar sprang onto a table, a pistol in each hand, his eyelids lowered. He was firing from the instant he leaped. Two bullets left the barrels together. Two targets erased. Before the bullets even arrived, he had removed those two targets from his mind.
Ten guns swung toward him and opened fire together. Wood chips flew from the tables and chairs around him.
Caesar leaped from the table into the air. During that airborne instant, in less than a second, each Desert Eagle fired twice, approaching the limits of those weapons.
Four more targets were erased from his mind. Six remained.

He landed on the table again. Six guns were trained on him; there was no room left to dodge. Fire from five guns sliced through the oak tables and chairs toward him, five overlapping barrages, no escape.
Suddenly the entire hall went dark. Every light went out. Before the afterimages had faded, Caesar vanished.
“My turn,” he said in the darkness.
Six rapidly accelerating heartbeats in the dark.
The Desert Eagles’ muzzle flashes flared and died. Each illuminated Caesar’s sharp profile, as though he stood amid the fires of hell.

The lights came on again. Caesar stood where he had been, arms lowered, two wisps of smoke rising from his pistols. Forty-six members of Team B and eleven intruders silently stared at their chests. Blood mist spurted, and they sagged to the floor. Every one of them had been shot through the chest. Fifty-seven weapons struck the ground in what sounded like a single crash.
Both sides had suffered heavy losses.
Gunfire still echoed in the hall when a solitary pair of hands began to clap.
“Not bad. You surprised me.” Mai was applauding.
Caesar ejected both magazines and removed the remaining rounds. Two remained in his left hand, one in his right.

“Desert Eagles. Standard seven-round magazines, .50-caliber AE ammunition. I used eleven rounds to deal with your eleven people.” He tossed the three remaining cartridges onto the table. “You changed the ending of the music. Otherwise your side would have lost.”
“Not on purpose. The piece was too sad. I’ve never liked sad endings.” Mai spread her hands. “It’s too soon to talk about winning and losing. I haven’t fired yet.”
No smoke rose from the muzzle of Mai’s Glock. She had aimed at Caesar, but never pulled the trigger.
Caesar glanced back at his fallen companions. “Frigga rounds? Apparently you aren’t looking to cause too many casualties.”
Everyone on both sides was merely unconscious. Without consulting each other, both sides had loaded anesthetic Frigga rounds.

Several paces apart, keeping a constant distance between them, the two strolled through Valhalla’s great hall, their eyes fixed on each other’s gun hands. Apart from the four guns, the atmosphere between them could have been called amicable.
“I see,” Mai said. “Your Yanling is Kamaitachi. No wonder you were confident. You’d already ordered the system to turn out the lights, and Kamaitachi is almost invincible in the dark.”
Yanling: Kamaitachi. Sequence number fifty-nine.

Kamaitachi were wind demons of Japanese mythology, three brothers who hid in the wind and slashed passersby with vacuums formed by high-speed air currents. With the Yanling named for them, the user commanded the wind within his domain. As if enslaved, it gathered every sound and brought it to him. Even in darkness without a trace of light, he used the wind as his eyes and retained command of the entire battlefield.
“You’re too kind. It seems you’re in no hurry to break into the underground level,” Caesar said.

“As you said, I have other companions. Right now your Executive Department’s elite are all away. Among the students, you and Chu Zihang have the greatest fighting ability. Your bloodlines would give us a great deal of trouble. My assignment is to keep you occupied. I can leave everything else to that three-nothings girl who never comes back empty-handed.”
“May I ask what a ‘three-nothings girl’ is?”

“A girl with no figure, no looks, and no enthusiasm. My exact opposite,” Mai said. (Author’s note: “Three-nothings girl” actually refers to a female character in Japanese anime who has “no words, no heart, and no expression,” such as Rei Ayanami. Mai is lying to Caesar here.)
“Then, facing such a beautiful opponent, I seem to have been luckier than Chu Zihang,” Caesar said mildly.
“Shall we see who draws faster?”
“All right.”
“With the lights out?” Mai gave a cold smile. “I’ll give you that advantage. Darkness is your home ground. We’ll compete on your turf.”
“All right,” Caesar said.
“Give me a moment.” Mai put her Glock on a nearby table and took two silver hair cuffs from an inside pocket.

Ignoring everyone, she smoothed the long locks beside her face. She had grown them specially: two feet long and black as lacquer, like an ancient Japanese woman in an ukiyo-e print. Paired with the athletic look of her high ponytail, those two long locks were very striking.
“You’re such a courteous man. It would be a shame to kill you.” Mai Sakatoku fastened a silver cuff to the end of each smoothed lock. Beautiful butterflies were engraved on the cuffs.
“In my family, men are taught always to be patient while a lady attends to her appearance,” Caesar said.
Caesar reloaded his magazines; Mai picked up her Glock. Both bowed their heads over their weapons, chambered rounds in the same instant, and raised their heads.
Caesar spread his arms like an eagle’s wings. “Caesar Gattuso, Cassell College. As you Japanese would put it: reporting for battle.”
“What year are you?” Mai suddenly asked.
Caesar blinked. “Third.”

“Oh. Mai Sakatoku, music department, University of Tokyo. Recipient of the mayoral scholarship, graduated a full two years ago. Reporting for battle.” Mai’s crimson brows lifted. “A third-year, and you already have ‘I think I’m cool’ written all over your face. But to me, you’re still just a junior. Give up now and call me ‘big sis,’ and I’ll let you off.”
Caesar remained coldly silent, a flash of frightening anger in his ice-blue eyes.
“Apparently you’re not the type with much of a sense of humor.” Mai shrugged and spun, the long locks with their silver cuffs whirling behind her.
“Ready!” She lowered herself into a crouch, then went utterly still.
“Norma, lights out.” Caesar snapped his fingers.
“Five-second countdown.” Norma’s voice echoed through Valhalla. The crystal chandeliers began blinking on and off, once per second.
Five, four, three, two, one… darkness!

In an instant, Caesar pushed Yanling: Kamaitachi to its peak, opening his domain to its fullest extent. He issued his command, and the Kamaitachi danced wildly through the air. Sound surged toward him like a raging tide. From the crackle of electrical sparks as the power cut out to the infrasonic waves formed by wind passing through Mai Sakatoku’s hair, it all overlapped, amplified hundreds and thousands of times, until Caesar seemed to stand inside a thundercloud.
Within Kamaitachi’s domain he was invincible, unless his opponent could attack faster than sound.

A faint tremor passed through his body. The Desert Eagles pointing ahead did not fire. Among the sounds Kamaitachi had gathered was something unexpected. It was like wind passing over the holes of a flute. There were two sources, like two wind spirits whirling through the air.

Mai’s two silver hair cuffs! The instant Caesar understood, the sound changed, turning cold and shrill, like ghosts wailing. Mai’s heartbeat was severed by those two sounds and dispersed into the air.
For the first time in his life, Kamaitachi had lost its target!
At the chapel, someone knocked on the door.

Someone opened it, closed it again, and walked into the chapel with footsteps so steady they were almost dull. The newcomer finally stopped in the exact center of the chapel. Chu Zihang opened the confessional door.

The two studied each other. Chu Zihang wore his school uniform with every button undone and held Murasame. His long black hair was loose, falling untidily over his face. The newcomer was entirely covered by a black combat uniform, including her head and face, but it was still evident she was a girl, only about 1.6 meters tall, yet decidedly curvaceous. Her stance, however—hands hanging straight against the sides of her legs, head slightly bowed—resembled a dutiful student who did nothing but study. There was nothing about it to stir anyone’s interest.
Neither opponent seemed willing to break the silence. Perhaps it was their personalities. There was none of Valhalla’s fiery enthusiasm here. It was dull beyond belief.
Chu Zihang coughed. “Are you the ‘three-nothings girl’?”
“Is that what Mai called me? Then I suppose so.” The three-nothings girl accepted her designation.
Chu Zihang closed his phone and set it beside him. “Caesar left his phone on, so I know how the battle over there is going.”
“So you aren’t at each other’s throats when you face an enemy. Is it over there?”
“They’re both still standing.”
“Oh.” The three-nothings girl paused. “I’m your opponent.”
“I know.”
She studied Chu Zihang’s face. Wind lifted his long hair, revealing those terrifying golden eyes. “You stayed to face the enemy alone because you didn’t want anyone to see you like this?”
“Yes.”
“Does someone like you ever find living in this world… contradictory?”
“Not particularly.”
Another long silence. Neither was much of a conversationalist. Every new topic required them to rack their brains.
“What… are they doing? Can banter really get this illogical?” Manstein swallowed nervously.
In the library control room, Schneider, Guderian, and Manstein were listening to events in the chapel. All three frowned at the exchange.

“We are a college with strict regulations. Our students should have discipline!” Manstein sounded heartbroken. “But look at what our elites are doing! Caesar Gattuso, president of the Student Council, is playing cowboy quick-draw games with his opponent. Is he trying to charm that long-legged woman? And Chu Zihang, president of the Lionheart Society, is chatting with the enemy! We can’t wait any longer. We should send reinforcements immediately and end the fighting!”
“I understand both Caesar’s and Chu Zihang’s actions,” Schneider said. “They’re learning about the enemy.”

“Do they need to spend time learning about the enemy at a moment like this? Their opponents must have dragon blood, or they couldn’t possibly face those two head-on,” Manstein said. “The bloodline advantages of both sides are evenly matched. We can’t take the risk!”
“No.” Schneider shook his head. “Have you noticed? Neither opponent seems to be in much of a hurry, whether in Valhalla or the chapel.”
“They’re stalling!” Guderian suddenly understood.
“Exactly! So it’s the library where we need to concentrate our defenses now, to seal off the final entrance.” Schneider pointed at the screen. A great many dots were converging on the library.

“Is that necessary? Norma directly controls the Verdandi area. There’s no possibility of a breach,” Manstein said. “We should still reinforce Caesar and Chu Zihang. They may be outstanding even among A-ranks, but if they slip up, it’ll be too late to repair the mistake.”
“I’ve already sent Team D to reinforce Valhalla. As for Chu Zihang, I have confidence in him,” Schneider said. “Once he acts, he can end the fight quickly!”
“If there’s nothing else to say, let’s begin.” They heard Chu Zihang speak again.
“All right,” said the three-nothings girl.
“Yanling: Sovereign Flame.” As Chu Zihang finished speaking, a low chant began, its rhythm quickening until it rose into a ringing incantation.
“Sovereign Flame… that’s sequence number eighty-nine!” Sweat beaded on Guderian’s forehead. “He’s only a third-year. How can he use Sovereign Flame?”
“Bloodline advantage. That’s why he’s super-A-rank,” Schneider said. “With his Sovereign Flame, the chapel won’t be a problem.”

“A third-year student wielding Sovereign Flame is like a child on a motorcycle about to blow past the top of the speedometer… All we can do is be grateful he’s still on our side,” Manstein said. “This time I believe you. The chapel doesn’t need anyone else. Chu Zihang can handle it.”
“Very well. Yanling: Sovereign Flame,” the three-nothings girl said calmly.
All three professors went deathly pale. The next moment, they heard the very same Draconic words in a girl’s voice, gradually catching up with Chu Zihang’s incantation.
“All units, watch the chapel! Brace for a shock wave!” Schneider snatched up the microphone and shouted.

He rushed to the window and looked out. Light as searing as an arc welder’s flame shot through the chapel windows. Communications instantly cut out. Dust spread rapidly in every direction, and in a single moment the chapel was reduced to rigid structural elements: pillars and load-bearing walls.
A moment later, that welding-bright blaze erupted again.
A moment later… again!
“They’re… just blasting each other with Sovereign Flame? Isn’t that… a little too crude and direct?” Cold sweat covered Manstein’s forehead.
“If… even the destructive Yanling Sovereign Flame isn’t ours alone…” Schneider was sweating coldly too. “Who are they?”
The Skuld area.
“Very good. Release.” Someone clapped his hands.

The four mechanical arms withdrew, leaving the brass jar suspended steadily in a superconducting magnetic field within cryogenic liquid nitrogen. Half-meter-thick quartz-glass walls surrounded it. Like a developing fetus, it slept in its mother’s womb: this specially constructed oval quartz-glass enclosure.
“Perfect!” The researchers in white lab coats applauded.

“I am delighted to announce that the Dragon King Norton has been successfully captured.” Principal Anjou raised his glass. “We paid a heavy price to capture this first-generation dragon, one of the Four Monarchs. But it was worth it. Ladies and gentlemen, to those who gave their lives for our cause.”
The researchers raised their glasses with solemn faces.

“Over the past several thousand years,” the principal sighed, “we have used alchemical artifacts, edged weapons, and even evil sorcery in our struggle against the dragons, at the cost of terrible sacrifices. But humanity’s own limitations meant that, even after making those sacrifices, all we could achieve was to send the Dragon Kings into slumber. They would cocoon themselves, their powerful spirits surviving as they waited to rise again.”
“But now we have acquired a weapon—a weapon that can destroy them once and for all!” His voice rose. “That weapon is science!”
The researchers applauded together. For these inveterate laboratory hermits, such praise for the science to which they had devoted their lives was the greatest encouragement imaginable.

“Over a hundred years of research into dragon genetics, alchemical technology, and Yanling has also deepened our understanding of dragons. Until now, however, we have never obtained a perfect specimen. Living dragons and complete skeletons are extremely difficult to acquire. The only living specimen we captured was an immature hatchling, with limited research value.” The principal pointed at the brass jar isolated within its sealed glass chamber. “But today will be historic. Let us witness a miracle in the history of science. We are going to… dissect a Dragon King!”
Thunderous applause. Dissecting a Dragon King—perhaps only dissecting an alien at Area 51 in Nevada could compare.
“Principal, is there a living specimen inside the brass jar?” A researcher raised a hand.

“We can’t be certain. The brass jar was cast around AD 33. It is a bone vessel. Its owner was Li Xiong, a minister of Gongsun Shu, the ruler of Sichuan in China at the time. Li Xiong urged Gongsun Shu to proclaim himself emperor and showed him the miracle of ‘a dragon appearing before the palace.’ Gongsun Shu consequently assumed the imperial title and named his era ‘Longxing,’ or ‘Dragon Rising.’ Li Xiong believed that, according to the Chinese theory of the elements, Gongsun Shu represented the west and belonged to metal. He made a curious prophecy: ‘Eight and the private mark; child and thread. Twelve shall be the term.’ It was an ill omen. The characters for ‘eight’ and the ‘private’ component combine to form ‘Gong,’ while ‘child’ and ‘thread’ signify ‘Sun.’ ‘Twelve shall be the term’ meant that Gongsun Shu’s reign would last only twelve years. Sure enough, twelve years later, Gongsun Shu died at the hands of another Chinese ruler, Liu Xiu. History, however, records no end for Li Xiong.” The principal stared at the jar. “Li Xiong cast that brass jar as his own coffin. It was also his egg, for incubating a new body. He placed it deep inside the bronze city to prevent outsiders from discovering it. Li Xiong was another name for the Dragon King Norton. He had crossed the Eurasian continent to China.”
“Is this bone vessel—or egg—safe?” Another hand rose.

“Yes. This jar isn’t actually made of brass, but of an unknown alchemical material. Norton is the King of Bronze and Fire. Both flame and metal are powerful forces that can awaken him, with the exception of the egg itself. So whatever seals him away must never be metal. That is also why we designed this quartz-glass chamber to hold him. He is now at a low temperature, in a metal-free environment, suspended by a uniform, powerful magnetic field.” The principal paused. “Such is the power of science!”
“We must not repeat the mistake of a hundred years ago,” he said quietly.

The researchers did not understand his last remark. They simply kept applauding. All the scientists were filled with anticipation, fortunate enough to witness this great moment in the history of science.
“Principal, what is that opening in the brass jar?” Someone had noticed a split in the upper part of the jar, a dark crack extending into its interior.

“Professor Mans of the Executive Department applied gray tin solution to it. We acquired that liquid from an ancient Egyptian tomb. So far, it is the only liquid capable of corroding this alchemical material.” The principal hesitated. “Perhaps we should begin with an MRI scan.”
The results appeared on the enormous screen. In an instant, every face changed.
A tremendous chill fell over every heart. They realized their optimism had been premature.
“Two chambers,” someone said quietly.
“One empty!” someone else said.

The jar’s internal structure was clearly visible, divided into two halves. Something resembling an enormous fetus curled inside one half; the other was empty. The disturbing crack lay directly above the empty chamber.
“Something… escaped from inside,” the principal said softly. “Damn it. Gray tin solution didn’t cause that opening… It’s an old wound. It’s… the crack in a dragon’s egg!”
He left his final thought unspoken: “The crack made when a dragon’s egg hatches!”
Number 13 stood among the crowd, now an assistant laboratory technician in a mask.

Everything had gone so smoothly. The signs had been wonderfully considerate, and eventually he had entered an enormous integrated laboratory. A group of men were showering in a bathroom, excitedly discussing some new arrival. Number 13 had shrewdly realized that it might be his target. After a little thought, he stripped off every stitch of clothing and walked straight into the steaming showers.

Dozens of naked men stood amid the white vapor. Number 13 went to a corner, greeted the man showering there, then knocked him unconscious with a single blow and hid him, still naked, in a locker. A sealed plastic bag in the locker held a sterile suit. Dressed in it from head to toe, he was so thoroughly protected that he looked ready to land on the moon.
Number 13 realized that what happened next was going to make him very excited.
Not the great moment in the history of science, but… five million US dollars.

So far, so good. In this sealed glass laboratory, everyone was beside themselves with excitement, and no one noticed an assistant technician like him. He had even lifted his mask to drink a celebratory glass of champagne. He was an easygoing fellow: when others nodded, he nodded; when they applauded, he applauded; when they drank, he drank.
Now he was merely waiting for a suitable chance to move closer and “observe the jar with his naked eyes,” so he could go back and write his report.
“Dissect it immediately,” the principal said. “Whatever the circumstances, this is an opportunity that comes once in a thousand years. We cannot delay.”
“Prepare the dissection instrument cart,” he said.

Number 13’s heart practically bloomed with joy. It was like wanting a nap and having someone toss him a pillow. He happened to be pushing that very cart, which carried an assortment of transparent tools made from nanomaterials.
“For safety, only the person responsible for the instruments will enter. We’ll leave the rest to the machines.” The principal turned to Number 13 with an expectant expression. “Ready?”

Number 13 could only nod vigorously. He had no idea what these people meant by a Dragon King. He had dissected a frog in high school biology… but that knowledge probably wouldn’t get him through this. Fortunately, he still had his sawed-off shotgun and a few thoroughly soaked shells tucked beneath his sterile suit. They gave him a little confidence.
The cryogenic chamber’s door slid open. White vapor from evaporating liquid nitrogen billowed out across his mask. Number 13 felt wave after wave of cold.

Everything in the cryogenic chamber was white. Liquid nitrogen vapor drifted around his feet. Fluorescent blue lights blinked. At the very center stood the oval quartz-glass enclosure, with the enormous brass jar inside.
For an instant, he had the illusion that he was standing on a boundless snowfield. From somewhere beyond the reach of his eyes came a soft call: “Brother.”
